One and a half years earlier, this 61-year-old woman had developed chronically progressive painful stiffness of the musculature of her body, sparing arms and facial musculature. This stiffness initially included only the legs, but spread subsequently to the abdomen, back and neck. Eventually, the patient could not walk or even sit. In addition, she complained of startle reactions with suddenly increasing muscle stiffness caused by unexpected acoustic, visual or tactile stimuli.

Symptomatic treatment with continuous intrathecal application of baclofen administered by a subcutaneous pump resulted in rapid clinical improvement so that the patient became ambulatory.
Clonazepam and baclofen were then given orally at dosages of 1. 5 mg and 20 mg daily, respectively, leading to improved mobility and relief of painful spasms.
Furthermore, effective immunosuppressive therapy with azathioprine (lymphocytes < 1000/gl) was initiated about 10 weeks after the start of the baclofen treatment.

After a 12-month course of continuous treatment the patient had improved further: the gait pattern had normalized and only one crutch was needed (Fig. 1). At that time GAD autoantibodies were still detected in serum but were only weakly present in CSF. After 24 months her condition had stabilized further: gait was now normal, without crutches.
